newsitem.title: USA: STG DENTED BUT OUTLOOK STILL POSITIVE - US EXPERTS.
newsitem.headline: STG DENTED BUT OUTLOOK STILL POSITIVE - US EXPERTS.

text.p: The British pound may not have the support of additional interest rate hikes in the months ahead, but the UK currency remains the unit of choice in Europe and its prospects remain bright, U.S. experts said.

The Bank of England raised official interest rates by 25 basis points on Thursday -- its fourth rate hike since May -- but signalled that additional hikes may not be necessary, sending sterling sharply lower against the dollar and the mark.

This weakness should prove fleeting, however, given the continued strength of Britain's economy and comparative sluggishness in the economies of its European counterparts across the Channel, economists said.
"We're still quite positive on the sterling against the European currencies," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities.
"Even if UK interest rates may have stopped going up they're still 400 basis points above German interest rates and the UK economy is still quite strong," he added.

Cable dipped to a 10-month low in U.S. trade following the Bank of England's fourth rate hike since May, its slide exacerbated by post-rate hike remarks that suggested rates were now in line with inflation targets.

In its statement, the British central bank said upward pressures on the sterling exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that rates had hit a level consistent with the bank's 2.5 percent inflation rate forecast.
Sterling/mark fell sharply from its high of 3.0285 to a trough of 2.9640 on Thursday.

Against the dollar, the pound traded as low as $1.5780 on Thursday before recovering a cent to $1.5880 by the U.S. afternoon. But damage sustained on Thursday is not a sign of things to come, analysts said.

Iggo said the pound could find support near its lows of the day, and called for a near-term range between $1.5750 and $1.6000. But strong UK economic fundamentals may prevent any broad moves lower, he said.
Other economists called the down-move primarily a correction from overvalued levels against the mark and forecast little additional damage.

That could change if recent interest rate hikes begin to take their toll on the UK economy later this year, but many economists feel recent credit tightening is unlikely to go far enough in curbing rampant consumer spending over the long haul.

"It remains an open question -- the direction for British rates -- it could be in three months time we find that the retail sector really is holding in there very strongly despite the higher interest rates, said Chris Widness, international economist at Chase Securities.
"At the same time (exports) may not be slowing as much as (some fear) because of sterling strength," he said.

Even with the rate hikes, Iggo contended that current official interest rates of 7.0 percent were not terribly high given the strength of domestic demand. In fact, he said rates will likely rise further, although perhaps not in the immediate future.
J.P. Morgan Securities has maintained its forecast for higher UK rates -- another 100 basis points within the next six months -- in spite of Thursday's statement from the Bank of England.
In the near-term, however, a failure to close the week above $1.5900 could portend near-term cable losses, said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan.
"While sterling is probably unsustainable at these levels, in the long-run it seems early -- given what we are expecting on rates -- for sterling to start going into a major decline," Leven said.
